title: Work, Wages & Chain Rule
shortDescription: Label every quantity as direct or inverse before you write a single equation — get the direction wrong and the chain rule flips your answer.
genZNote: More workers, fewer days — that's inverse. More hours, more work — that's direct. Label each pair before you touch the numbers, or the chain rule will flip on you.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: The Chain Rule generalises simple proportion to problems with multiple linked quantities (workers, days, hours/day, units of work, wages) changing simultaneously. The essential first step: label each pairwise relationship as either DIRECT variation (both increase/decrease together) or INVERSE variation (one increases as the other decreases) BEFORE setting up any equation.

sections.heading: Direct vs. Inverse — How to Tell
bullets: More workers, same work → FEWER days needed: inverse.
More hours worked per day → MORE work done in the same number of days: direct.
More days worked, same rate of pay per day → MORE total wages: direct.
More workers sharing a fixed total wage for the same job → LESS wage per individual worker: inverse.

sections.heading: Worked Example — Standard vs Fast Method

steps.name: Standard method
steps.explanation: 12 workers complete a job in 8 days working 6 hours/day. How many days will 16 workers take, working 8 hours/day, for the same job? Total worker-hours is fixed: 12×8×6 = 16×D×8.
steps.purpose: Set total worker-hours (workers × days × hours) as a fixed quantity, since the total amount of work is unchanged.

steps.name: Fast method — solve the ratio directly
steps.purpose: Cancel common factors between numerator and denominator before multiplying out, to keep the numbers small.

sections.heading: Wages Proportional to Work Done
sections.body: If wages are shared among workers, the share is proportional to the AMOUNT of work each person actually contributes — which itself depends on their efficiency and the time/days they worked, not headcount alone. If workers have different efficiencies, replace a straight headcount ratio with an efficiency-weighted ratio (similar to the Partnership capital-time approach, but using efficiency×time instead of capital×time).

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Treating every quantity in a chain-rule problem as directly proportional — some relationships (like workers vs. days needed for fixed total work) are inversely proportional; mislabelling the direction inverts the final answer.
Forgetting that when efficiency differs between workers, a straight headcount ratio must be replaced with an efficiency-weighted one.
Not cancelling common factors before multiplying out a multi-quantity chain — this makes arithmetic errors far more likely.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Write direct/inverse labels next to every pair of changing quantities before setting up the equation — this single step prevents the most common chain-rule mistake.
Set up the problem as 'total work is fixed' (workers × days × hours = constant) whenever the same job is being completed under different conditions.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Chain Rule links multiple varying quantities via direct or inverse proportion; label each pairwise relationship before setting up the equation.
keyFacts: Direct: both quantities increase/decrease together. Inverse: one increases as the other decreases.
Workers × Days × Hours/day = constant for a fixed total job.
Wages split by efficiency-weighted contribution when efficiency differs between workers.
commonConfusion: More workers means fewer days (inverse) but more total wages paid overall for the same daily rate (direct) — two different relationships hiding in the same sentence.

highYieldFacts: Workers × Days × Hours/day = constant is the standard chain-rule setup for a fixed total job.
Efficiency differences require an efficiency-weighted ratio, not a plain headcount ratio.
commonTraps: Mislabelling a direct relationship as inverse or vice versa.
Ignoring efficiency differences and using a plain headcount ratio to split wages.
mustRemember: Label direct vs inverse for every pair of quantities before writing the equation.
